concept.name: Price-to-book ratio
concept.definition: Market capitalization - or price per share - divided by the book value of shareholders' equity: what investors pay per dollar of net asset value on the balance sheet. Damodaran's consistency rule for multiples requires equity value in the numerator to be paired with equity book value in the denominator.
concept.intuition: P/B asks whether the market values the business above or below the accumulated accounting value of what it owns minus what it owes.
concept.mechanics: Divide price per share by book value per share (shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding). The ratio links fundamentally to return on equity: firms earning ROE above their cost of equity deserve to trade above book value.
concept.formula: P/B = Price per share / Book value per share; for a stable-growth firm, P/B = ROE x Payout ratio / (r - g).
concept.failure_modes: Book value omits intangibles such as brands, software, and R&D, so P/B misleads for asset-light firms; heavy buybacks or losses can shrink equity to the point of absurd ratios.
concept.misconceptions: A P/B below 1 is not automatically a bargain - it can mean the market expects the assets to earn below their cost of capital or to be written down.
concept.example: A bank trading at $12 per share with a book value of $10 per share has a P/B of 1.2; a software firm at the same multiple would be unusually cheap because its real assets are mostly off-balance-sheet.

citations.source: Aswath Damodaran (NYU Stern), Relative Valuation lecture notes (Packet 2)
citations.section: Definitional Tests: equity value over equity book value
